newsitem.title: UK: Mark crosses hold firmer tone but off highs.
newsitem.headline: Mark crosses hold firmer tone but off highs.

text.p: The mark held its firmer tone on the European crosses but was off its best levels as the trend continued to be dominated by moves in dollar/mark, dealers said.
"The direction of the cross trading is being dictated by dollar/mark dynamics which today will take its clue from the U.S. trade figures," said one trader.
"Another poor deficit could see further mark gains."
The data are due at 1230 GMT and expected to show a February trade shortfall of around $10 billion compared with a $12.7 billion deficit in January.

The mark earlier hit a 14-week high on the Norwegian crown and was firm on the Swedish crown as the Swedish currency continued to be dogged by post budget blues. The Norwegian crown was simply being dragged down by the Swedish crown, dealers said.
At 1017 GMT the mark was at 4.4655/85 Swedish crowns after a 4.4735 high and at 4.0900/30 Norwegian crowns after a high of 4.1110.
Traders also noted some talk of options related selling of the Norwegian crown.
The west German business climate index fell to 92.4 in March compared with 93.6 in February, wall below expectations for a 94.0 figure.
Dealers said the figure has done nothing to dispel the idea that interest rate differentials will continue to favour the dollar.
Mark/lira was at 984.85/5.35, little changed from a previous 985.00/30. The Italian government faces a new confidence vote at 1700 GMT over draft law covering civil service reforms.
This is the second confidence vote in as many weeks and the last pushed the year-old administration of Prime Minister Romano Prodi to the brink of collapse.

The Italian Il Sole 24 Ore newspaper said on Thursday that Germany and France will try to reach a consensus by September this year on which European countries will be able to qualify for a single currency from start in 1999.
Chances of European currency union starting on time seem to be improving because fewer countries are expected to qualify from the outset, a Reuters survey published on Thursday showed.

Forty three analysts predicted the likelihood of EMU going ahead on time on January 1, 1999. The average response gave EMU an 80 percent chance of starting on time, up from 76 percent in March. In February, the average prediction was 83 percent.
